newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch labour market reasonably flexible - CPB.
newsitem.headline: Dutch labour market reasonably flexible - CPB.

text.p: The Dutch labour market is reasonably flexible and strongly committed to good relations between employers and employees, the Dutch Central Planning Bureau (CPB) said on Wednesday.

Dutch labour market institutions seemed better adapted to trends in the world economy than their German counterparts, the CPB concluded from a study comparing the German, Dutch and American labour markets.
The study focused on the capacity for adjustment in these markets and the degree to which market institutions stimulated good labour relations between employers and employees.
"Long-term trends of the world economy increase the importance of both flexibility and commitment," the CPB said.
"Competition in high-quality markets demands an increasing amount of (company) specific knowledge, ... while the importance of flexible employment and wages also rises."
The CPB said the German labour market was less flexible than the Dutch model.
The model was so focused on commitment, that the German economy's capacity to adapt to fast changing external circumstances was reduced, it said.
"Combining flexibility and commitment, the Dutch labour market model is situated in between the German and the American (models)," the CPB said.
The American model promotes flexibility, often at the expense of job and income security, sometimes making employees less committed to their employment relationships.
The Dutch model includes wide-ranging protection against dismissal and the opportunity for employees to formally participate in decision-making processes.
But it remained more flexible than the German model.

The relatively high percentage of part-time and temporary workers in the Netherlands enabled employers to meet cyclical variations in their staffing needs, while centralised wage negotiations produced salaries that were more finely tuned to macro economic cycles than in Germany.

The CPB said agreements between major companies and trade union on working conditions and remuneration now covered 13 percent of Dutch workers, producing a more varied scale of wages than in other nations.
But in Germany, such wage negotiations were largely conducted at sector level.
